title: The Stations of the Cross
hook: fourteen stops along the way of the cross, prayed in some churches

segments.voice: Yesterday, vesture: a table cleared to the wood while a psalm was read in the dark. Your line was bare.

Along the side walls of some churches hang small carvings or paintings, spaced out like mile markers. A man standing before a judge. A woman holding out a cloth. A stranger pulled from the crowd to carry a beam of wood. On Good Friday, and in some churches on other Fridays too, people walk from one to the next. They stop, they pray, they move on. In Jerusalem, pilgrims walk a route through the old streets that tradition calls the way of sorrows, stopping at the same scenes. On a church wall, the walk comes to wherever you live. Today, the Stations of the Cross.

The stations are a walk with stops. Tradition counts fourteen in the usual set, from Jesus condemned to his body laid in the tomb. Some come straight from the Gospels; others come from tradition. Take one from the Gospels first. Luke says that as they led Jesus away, the soldiers grabbed a passerby. In the King James: "they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus." A man on his way into the city ends up walking directly behind Jesus with the weight on his shoulders. Some readers hear in that phrase, after Jesus, the language of following. A little further on, Luke has women in the crowd weeping, and Jesus turns to them: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Even on that road he turns to face them, and his words point past his own suffering to troubles still ahead for the city and its children. Other stations, like Jesus falling under the cross, or a woman named Veronica wiping his face, come from tradition rather than the Gospel text. The stations are prayed in Catholic and Anglican churches, and in some others. Some versions use only scenes found in the Gospels, and some Protestants prefer it that way. Whichever set is used, the shape is the same: you walk a few steps, stop at one moment, stay with it, then walk again. The story at walking pace.
screen: `SOME FROM THE GOSPELS, SOME FROM TRADITION.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly around the room, down a hallway, or in place, and stop now and then for one breath, fourteen times if you like, without counting too carefully. At each stop, let one face come to mind, someone carrying something heavy right now, and hold them there for a breath the way Simon held the beam; if you pray, name each one to God.
Cyrenian. The name for Simon, the passerby soldiers pulled from the crowd to carry Jesus's cross, walking it one station at a time.
Your line: step by step with him. One stop, then the next. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics, Anglicans and some other Christians pray the Stations of the Cross, especially on Good Friday, walking from station to station in church with a short reading and prayer at each.

chat.says: Are all the Stations of the Cross from the Bible?
options: Some, like Simon carrying the cross; others, like Veronica, are tradition.
Yes, all fourteen are scenes told in the Gospels, word for word.
No, none are; they were all invented for pilgrims in Jerusalem.
chat.meaning: Tradition counts fourteen stations. Some, like Simon carrying the cross, come from the Gospels; Jesus's falls and Veronica come from tradition.

Cyrenian.meaning: Luke's name for Simon, the man who carried the cross

Veronica.meaning: a woman who, tradition says, wiped Jesus's face

way of sorrows.meaning: a Jerusalem route that tradition says Jesus walked

Daughters of Jerusalem.meaning: the weeping women Jesus turns to on the road

notes: Claims rule: the number fourteen is attributed to tradition ('tradition counts fourteen in the usual set'); no history or dates of the devotion are given. The practice's fourteen pauses follow the outline.
Veronica and Jesus's falls are named as coming from tradition, not the Gospels; meeting his mother is not mentioned. Confirm wording is respectful to Catholic Keepers.
Which churches pray the stations (Catholics, Anglicans, 'some other churches') and that some versions use only scriptural scenes, preferred by 'some Protestants', should be confirmed.
The Via Dolorosa is described only as 'a route through the old streets that tradition calls the way of sorrows'; confirm.
Editor pass: the 'language of following' reading of Luke 23:26 is now attributed to some readers rather than stated as fact.
Second editor pass: cut the unsourced 'and churches say so plainly'; the line on who prays the stations no longer reads as every Catholic and Anglican.
Audit pass: Luke 23:28 was read as Jesus attending to the women's grief; in context (23:29–31) it is a warning of coming disaster for Jerusalem, and the line now says so.
